title: ANTH418 Assignment 5: Teotihuacan Leporid Management
text:
Case study
Somerville, Andrew D., Nawa Sugiyama, Linda R. Manzanilla, and Margaret J. Schoeninger. 2016. Animal Management at the Ancient Metropolis of Teotihuacan, Mexico: Stable Isotope Analysis of Leporid (Cottontail and Jackrabbit) Bone Mineral. PLOS ONE 11(8): e0159982.
This two-context comparison is a teaching exercise using published observations; it is not a reproduction of the full statistical analysis in Somerville et al. (2016).
Before beginning, read README.md, codebook.md, and provenance.md.

library(tidyverse)
library(infer)

data_path <- if (file.exists("data/teotihuacan_leporids.csv")) {
  "data/teotihuacan_leporids.csv"
} else {
  "assignments/assignment05_teotihuacan_inference/data/teotihuacan_leporids.csv"
}

dat <- read_csv(
  data_path,
  show_col_types = FALSE
) |>
  filter(valid)

d <- dat |>
  filter(
    context %in% c(
      "Oztoyahualco",
      "Moon Pyramid"
    )
  )

d |> count(context)

  context          n

1 Moon Pyramid    50
2 Oztoyahualco    15

4. Bootstrap confidence interval
Set the random seed:

set.seed(418)

Using infer, generate 10,000 bootstrap resamples and calculate the difference in means in the same direction:
Oztoyahualco − Moon Pyramid
Construct a 95% percentile bootstrap confidence interval.

Visualize the bootstrap distribution and mark the confidence interval.

lower confidence bound;

5. Specify the null model
For this comparison, use:
\[
H_0:
\mu_{\text{Oztoyahualco}}
-
\mu_{\text{Moon Pyramid}}
=0
\]
and the two-sided alternative:
\[
H_A:
\mu_{\text{Oztoyahualco}}
-

\neq0.
\]
In words, under the null model, context carries no systematic information about δ13C for this comparison.

set.seed(418)

Under the no-association null model, use infer to generate 10,000 permutations of the context labels.
Calculate the difference in means for every permutation.

Calculate a two-sided permutation p-value using permuted statistics at least as extreme as the observed statistic.

the observed difference in means;
the 95% bootstrap confidence interval;
the two-sided permutation p-value.

Answer:

How large is the observed contrast?
How uncertain is the estimate?
What range of differences is compatible with the data under the bootstrap procedure?
How unusual is the observed difference under the permutation null model?

title: ANTH418 Assignment 3: Missing Data in the Seshat Moralizing Gods Debate
text:
NoteBefore you begin



Read the Week 6 Study Guide before starting this assignment.
The Study Guide explains the required concepts and R workflow for data transformation, missing values, the distinction between NA and a recorded zero, deletion and imputation as analytical decisions, and sensitivity analysis.
This assignment uses a deliberately small aggregated teaching dataset. The CSV contains three rows summarizing the outcome status of the 801 observations in the documented Seshat regression frame. It does not contain 801 individual rows.

title: ANTH418 Assignment 3: Missing Data in the Seshat Moralizing Gods Debate
text:
Research question
How does treating unknown observations as known absences change the descriptive pattern of moralizing-gods outcomes in the documented Seshat regression frame?

title: ANTH418 Assignment 3: Missing Data in the Seshat Moralizing Gods Debate
text:
Case Study
Seshat: Global History Databank was developed to organize historical and archaeological information about past societies in standardized form for large-scale comparative research (Turchin et al. 2015).
Whitehouse et al. (2019) used Seshat data to investigate the relationship between social complexity and moralizing gods. Their published analysis argued that moralizing gods generally appeared after large increases in social complexity.
Beheim et al. (2021) subsequently focused attention on the treatment of missing outcome data. In the documented 801-observation regression frame, they reported:

299 observations in which moralizing gods were recorded as present;
12 observations in which moralizing gods were recorded as absent; and
490 observations in which the outcome was missing or unknown.

The critical issue is that the 490 unknown observations were treated in the disputed analysis as if they were known absences.
This creates a fundamental data distinction:
documented absence is not the same thing as missing information.
The ANTH418 teaching file preserves these three states explicitly. Your task is not to reproduce the original regression models. Instead, you will use descriptive summaries and visualization to examine how the apparent empirical pattern changes when the 490 unknown observations are represented in two different ways.

title: ANTH418 Assignment 3: Missing Data in the Seshat Moralizing Gods Debate
text:
5. Compare the two representations
Create a compact comparison table.

comparison <- tibble(
  representation = c(
    "Unknown preserved",
    "Unknown preserved",
    "Unknown preserved",
    "Unknown recoded as absent",
    "Unknown recoded as absent"
  ),
  status = c(
    "Present",
    "Absent",
    "Unknown",
    "Present",
    "Absent"
  ),
  count = c(
    299,
    12,
    490,
    299,
    12 + 490
  )
) |>
  group_by(representation) |>
  mutate(
    percent = 100 * count / sum(count)
  ) |>
  ungroup()

comparison

# A tibble: 5 × 4
  representation            status  count percent
  <chr>                     <chr>   <dbl>   <dbl>
1 Unknown preserved         Present   299   37.3 
2 Unknown preserved         Absent     12    1.50
3 Unknown preserved         Unknown   490   61.2 
4 Unknown recoded as absent Present   299   37.3 
5 Unknown recoded as absent Absent    502   62.7 


Use the table to answer:

Does the number of documented presences change?
Does the amount of historical evidence change?
What changes when unknown cases are combined with documented absences?
How does the apparent balance between “present” and “absent” change?

The key question is not merely whether the percentages differ. Explain why they differ.

title: ANTH418 Assignment 3: Missing Data in the Seshat Moralizing Gods Debate
text:
6. Visualize the sensitivity analysis
Create a figure that allows the two representations to be compared directly.

ggplot(
  comparison,
  aes(x = status, y = percent)
) +
  geom_col() +
  facet_wrap(~ representation) +
  labs(
    x = "Outcome status",
    y = "Percentage of observations",
    title = "Effect of treating unknown outcomes as absences"
  )








Refine the plot so that the comparison is easy to read.

# Your code

Then interpret the figure. Address what remains unchanged, what changes dramatically, whether the change comes from new observations or recoding existing uncertainty, and why the two representations can produce different impressions of the historical pattern.






ImportantSensitivity analysis



A sensitivity analysis asks whether a substantive pattern changes when an important analytical choice changes.
If the interpretation changes substantially under an alternative reasonable treatment, the conclusion is sensitive to that decision. This does not by itself establish which treatment is historically correct.

title: ANTH418 Assignment 3: Missing Data in the Seshat Moralizing Gods Debate
text:
7. Interpret the analytical consequences
Write a concise interpretation bringing together your numerical summaries and visualizations.
Your discussion should explain:

why missing_unknown and known_absent represent different evidential states;
why the original three-category representation preserves information that the two-category recoding removes;
how the apparent proportion of absences changes under the recoding;
why this is a data-analysis decision rather than a purely technical formatting choice;
what the sensitivity comparison can establish; and
what it cannot establish about the actual historical presence or absence of moralizing gods.

Connect your interpretation to the broader Week 6 principle:

Preparation is analysis.

A recoding decision can change the empirical pattern presented to the reader even though the underlying documentary evidence has not changed.

Final interpretation guidance
Use these questions to structure your concluding paragraph:

What does the teaching file summarize?
What proportion of the underlying 801 observations is unknown?
What is the difference between a documented absence and an unknown outcome?
What happens numerically when the unknown cases are recoded as absent?
Does that operation add historical evidence?
Is the descriptive pattern sensitive to the coding decision?
What conclusion about data preparation can you draw from this case?
What historical conclusion would go beyond what this aggregated teaching dataset can establish?







WarningStatistical scope



This assignment is limited to descriptive missing-data analysis, visualization, recoding, and simple sensitivity analysis.
Do not perform t-tests, regression, Bayesian modeling, multiple imputation, MICE, or other inferential analyses. Do not attempt to reproduce the original Whitehouse et al. or Beheim et al. statistical models from this three-row teaching summary.

title: ANTH418 Assignment 1: Bronze Age Diet and Farming at La Bastida and Gatas
text:
Research question
How should the human stable-isotope distributions at La Bastida and Gatas be described, and what do different measures of center and dispersion reveal?

title: ANTH418 Assignment 1: Bronze Age Diet and Farming at La Bastida and Gatas
text:
Case Study
La Bastida and Gatas were settlements of the El Argar society (ca. 2200–1550 BCE) in southeastern Spain. Knipper et al. (2020) analyzed stable carbon (δ¹³C) and nitrogen (δ¹⁵N) isotope values from human and animal bone collagen and charred cereal grains to investigate diet, crop cultivation, and animal husbandry. The usable human dataset includes 48 individuals from La Bastida and 21 from Gatas.

title: ANTH418 Assignment 1: Bronze Age Diet and Farming at La Bastida and Gatas
text:
Assignment
Using the provided human isotope dataset, conduct a descriptive statistical comparison of δ¹³C and δ¹⁵N values from La Bastida and Gatas. The objective is to apply the measures of central tendency and dispersion introduced in Week 4 to a substantive archaeological problem. Use descriptive statistics to characterize both the typical values and the variability within each archaeological sample before interpreting differences between the two sites.
For each isotope and site, calculate the mean and median as measures of central tendency and the standard deviation, interquartile range (IQR), minimum, maximum, and range as measures of dispersion. Use appropriate histograms and boxplots to examine the shape and spread of the distributions, possible outliers, and the degree of overlap between the two sites. Based on these results, briefly describe the principal similarities and differences between La Bastida and Gatas.
Your interpretation should maintain a clear distinction between statistical description and archaeological explanation. In particular, differences in human isotope values should not be treated as direct evidence of differences in diet. Knipper et al. (2020) demonstrate that variation in cereal and animal isotope baselines and farming practices can contribute to differences in human isotope values; when these factors are considered, the two populations may have had broadly similar dietary compositions. Your task is therefore to establish what the observed distributions show before considering why those patterns may exist.

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
Statistical inference asks us to move from an observed sample to a larger population while remaining explicit about uncertainty. In archaeology, that move is especially difficult because specimens have already passed through preservation, deposition, excavation, recovery, curation, identification, and analytical selection.
This week follows one connected sequence:

Estimate → quantify uncertainty → test against a null model → interpret archaeologically

It forms three conceptual movements: (I) estimate and quantify uncertainty; (II) test against a null model; and (III) interpret archaeologically. Statistical inference is one component of archaeological inference, not a substitute for it.

Somerville, A. D., Sugiyama, N., Manzanilla, L. R., & Schoeninger, M. J. (2016). Animal management at the ancient metropolis of Teotihuacan, Mexico: Stable isotope analysis of leporid (cottontail and jackrabbit) bone mineral. PLOS ONE, 11(8), e0159982.
Thulin, M. (2024). Modern statistics with R: From wrangling and exploring data to inference and predictive modelling (2nd ed.). Chapman & Hall/CRC. Chapter 3 sections on hypothesis testing, p-values, and confidence intervals.

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
1. From Samples to Populations
A population is the larger set of cases about which we want to learn. A sample is the set we observe. A parameter describes a population; a statistic is calculated from a sample.



Population quantity
Sample estimate




Mean, \(\mu\)
Mean, \(\bar{x}\)


Variance, \(\sigma^2\)
Variance, \(s^2\)


Proportion, \(P\)
Proportion, \(\hat{p}\)


Difference, \(\mu_1-\mu_2\)
Difference, \(\bar{x}_1-\bar{x}_2\)



A parameter is treated as fixed but usually unknown. Sample statistics vary from sample to sample. This sampling variability is why estimates need an account of uncertainty (Cumming & Calin-Jageman, 2024).

Archaeological complication
Archaeological samples are rarely simple random samples. Before inference, ask:

What is the target population?
What exactly is the observed sample?
How did preservation, excavation, recovery, curation, and analytical selection produce it?
Which cases could not enter it?
What assumptions permit the sample to inform the population?


Key idea: More sophisticated statistics do not automatically make an archaeological sample representative.

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
2. Point Estimates versus Interval Estimates
A point estimate is a single numerical estimate. It answers “How much?” An interval estimate adds information about precision.
For a mean, a conventional confidence interval has the general form
\[
\bar{x} \pm t_{\mathrm{crit}}\times SE,
\qquad
SE=\frac{s}{\sqrt{n}}.
\]
The standard error describes how much an estimate such as the sample mean would vary across repeated samples. It is not the standard deviation of the individual observations.
Larger samples generally produce narrower intervals; greater variability generally produces wider intervals. But precision is not correctness: a narrow interval around a biased estimate can be precisely wrong.

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
section: 3. What Does a 95% Confidence Interval Mean?
text:
3. What Does a 95% Confidence Interval Mean?
In the standard frequentist interpretation, if the same sampling-and-interval procedure were repeated many times, about 95% of the resulting intervals would contain the fixed population parameter, assuming the method and assumptions are appropriate (Cumming & Calin-Jageman, 2024).
Do not say that a particular frequentist interval gives a 95% probability that the fixed parameter lies inside it.
Instead ask: Where is the estimate? How wide is the interval? Which effect magnitudes remain compatible with the data and assumptions? Are those magnitudes archaeologically meaningful?
Do not turn a confidence interval into another binary significance detector by looking only at whether it crosses zero.

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
section: 5. Estimation and Testing Ask Different Questions
text:
5. Estimation and Testing Ask Different Questions
Estimation asks: How large is the effect, and how uncertain is the estimate?
Testing asks: How unusual would the observed result be under a specified null model?
A useful analysis often needs both. Estimate first; then ask whether the observed pattern is unusual under a clearly defined reference model.

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
6. Null and Alternative Hypotheses
For two population means:
\[
H_0:\mu_1-\mu_2=0
\]
\[
H_A:\mu_1-\mu_2\neq0
\]
The null hypothesis is a statistical reference model. It is not necessarily an archaeological claim that “nothing happened.”
Likewise, “the population isotope means differ” is not equivalent to “people managed leporids.” The first is statistical; the second proposes human behavior. Moving between them requires archaeological theory, context, chronology, ecology, and alternatives.

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
7. Permutation Tests and Null Distributions
A permutation test constructs a null distribution by rearranging data in a way that represents the null hypothesis:

calculate the observed statistic;
keep measured values fixed;
shuffle group labels as permitted by the null model;
preserve group sizes;
recalculate the statistic;
repeat many times; and
locate the observed statistic in the resulting null distribution.


Permutation: What would differences look like if the null model held?

Its validity depends on exchangeability: which observations can legitimately have their labels shuffled?







Bootstrap
Permutation




Resample observations with replacement
Usually shuffle labels


Quantifies uncertainty in an estimate
Evaluates compatibility with a null model


Produces a bootstrap distribution
Produces a null distribution


Commonly supports confidence intervals
Commonly supports p-values



Both are resampling methods, but they answer different questions (Thulin, 2024).

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
8. p-Values as Tail Probabilities
A p-value is calculated under a specified null model:
\[
p=P(\text{result as extreme or more extreme}\mid H_0\text{ and assumptions}).
\]
A small p-value places the observed statistic relatively far into the tails of the null distribution. A large p-value means that the result is not unusual under that model; it does not prove the null is true.
A p-value is not the probability that \(H_0\) is true, the probability that \(H_A\) is true, the probability that chance caused the result, the probability that this result is a false positive, the effect size, or the probability that an archaeological explanation is correct (Cumming & Calin-Jageman, 2024; Hubbard, 2011).

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
9. Beyond the .05 Bright Line
Students need to understand the conventional p < .05 rule because it remains common. But it should not become a decision ritual. Wasserstein et al. (2019) argue against drawing conclusions solely from whether a p-value crosses an arbitrary threshold. Values such as p = .049 and p = .051 should not be treated as fundamentally different scientific outcomes.
A fuller interpretation combines:

Magnitude + uncertainty + context

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
10. Statistical Significance versus Archaeological Significance
Statistical significance concerns data relative to a statistical model and decision convention. Archaeological significance concerns what a pattern means for understanding past practices, institutions, environments, chronology, or other processes.
The two can diverge. A tiny effect can become statistically detectable in a large sample; an archaeologically important effect can remain uncertain in a small sample; and a strong-looking pattern can reflect biased sampling, chronological mixing, or non-independent observations.
The archaeological question is therefore not merely:

Is p < .05?

It is:

How large is the pattern, how uncertain is it, what archaeological process could generate it, and what other evidence makes that process more or less plausible?

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
11. The Archaeological Problem
Somerville et al. (2016) asked whether cottontails and jackrabbits at Teotihuacan were simply hunted or whether some were also provisioned, managed, or bred.
The case contains the full inferential chain:

archaeological question → measurement → comparison → uncertainty/testing → archaeological interpretation

The authors analyzed stable carbon and oxygen isotopes from leporid bone mineral. Greater consumption of C4/CAM plants—including maize and other plants associated with human cultivation—can elevate leporid \(\delta^{13}C\) values. But an isotope measurement is not a direct observation of someone feeding an animal.

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
12. Why Oztoyahualco Matters
Oztoyahualco 15B was archaeologically relevant before the isotope test. The compound contained an unusually large leporid assemblage and contextual evidence associated with animal processing and possible keeping (Somerville et al., 2016).
This motivates a prediction:

If leporids at Oztoyahualco were unusually integrated into human provisioning, their carbon isotope values should differ in the predicted direction from appropriate comparison contexts.

The statistical analysis therefore follows an archaeological question rather than searching for any contrast that happens to yield a small p-value.

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
13. Begin with the Estimate
Somerville et al. (2016) reported a mean \(\delta^{13}C_{apatite}\) of approximately −5.9‰ for Oztoyahualco leporids and approximately −8.3‰ for the combined other archaeological contexts: an observed contrast of about +2.4‰. Their dietary interpretation associated the Oztoyahualco mean with approximately 74% C4/CAM plant consumption.
Before asking whether the difference is “significant,” ask:

What is its direction and magnitude?
How variable are observations within groups?
How uncertain is the estimated contrast?
Is +2.4‰ meaningful in isotope-ecological terms?
Are the groups archaeologically and chronologically appropriate comparisons?

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
14. Test Against the Null
Somerville et al. (2016) reported that the Oztoyahualco \(\delta^{13}C_{apatite}\) mean was higher than the combined mean of the other archaeological locations (p = .001).
This does not mean there is a .1% probability that leporid management did not occur. The test addresses a statistical contrast relative to a null model; it does not assign a probability to the archaeological explanation.

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
15. Build the Archaeological Interpretation
The interpretive chain is approximately:
\[
\text{higher }\delta^{13}C
\rightarrow
\text{greater C4/CAM consumption}
\rightarrow
\text{access to cultivated resources}
\rightarrow
\text{possible provisioning}
\rightarrow
\text{possible management/breeding}.
\]
Every arrow requires evidence.
Somerville et al. (2016) strengthen the interpretation by combining isotopic results with archaeological context. Alternatives remain possible, including crop raiding, garden hunting, movement of animals, and mixtures of managed and wild animals.
The supplementary collagen study (Somerville et al., 2017) shows why binary significance is inadequate. Variation among animals, multiple leporid taxa, and isotope variance inconsistent with highly standardized production complicate a simple closed-system breeding model.

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
16. Sampling
A confidence interval can be numerically precise while representing the wrong population. Preservation, excavation strategy, recovery, curation, laboratory selection, and chronological aggregation affect what a sample can represent.

Ask: What population can these observations legitimately represent?

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
text:
17. Independence and Exchangeability
Archaeological observations are often clustered: several bones may derive from one animal, artifacts from one feature, features from one household, and households from one neighborhood. Treating correlated observations as independent inflates the apparent amount of information and may make uncertainty too small.
For permutation tests:

Ask: What exactly may legitimately be shuffled?

title: Week 8 — Confidence Intervals and Hypothesis Testing
section: 18. What a Statistical Test Cannot Establish
text:
18. What a Statistical Test Cannot Establish
A statistical test cannot by itself establish causation, mechanism, representativeness, correct chronology, correct measurement, or archaeological meaning. A small p-value cannot choose among competing archaeological explanations unless the research design and contextual evidence make those alternatives distinguishable.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text: Class meeting: 14 October 2026 Focus: data transformation · missing values · recoding · sensitivity analysis Case study: Seshat moralizing-gods debate Assessment: Assignment 3 — Missing Data in the Seshat Moralizing Gods Debate

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
Overview
Week 6 asks what happens before formal inference:

How can decisions made while preparing data change the conclusions we eventually draw?

Real anthropological and archaeological datasets may be skewed, measured on incompatible scales, or incomplete. Researchers therefore transform, recode, filter, and otherwise prepare data. These operations are necessary, but they are not neutral.






NoteThe Week 6 principle



Preparation is analysis. Every transformation or missing-data decision should have a substantive reason, remain visible in the code, and be checked for its effect on the empirical pattern.


The central case study is the Seshat moralizing-gods debate. Whitehouse et al. (2019) reported that moralizing gods tended to appear after large increases in social complexity. Beheim et al. (2021) showed that 61% of the moralizing-gods observations used in the analysis were missing and had been treated as known absences. Alternative treatments changed the reported pattern.
\[\texttt{NA} \neq 0\]

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
Questions

Why do researchers transform variables?
How do log, root, reciprocal, and standardizing transformations differ?
What does NA mean in R, and why is it different from 0?
What are explicit and implicit missingness?
What do MCAR, MAR, and MNAR mean?
What are the costs of deletion and simple imputation?
What is sensitivity analysis?
How can preparation decisions change anthropological conclusions?

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
Learning objectives
After this week, you should be able to diagnose reasons for transformation; create transformed variables without overwriting originals; identify and count missing values; distinguish unknown from documented absence; explain explicit/implicit missingness and MCAR/MAR/MNAR; recognize costs of deletion and single imputation; and compare alternative missing-data treatments with a simple sensitivity analysis.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
1. What is a transformation?
A transformation applies a mathematical function to a variable and creates a new numerical representation of the same observations.

assemblage_size <- c(5, 8, 12, 18, 35, 90, 250)
tibble(assemblage_size) |>
  mutate(log_assemblage_size = log(assemblage_size))

# A tibble: 7 × 2
  assemblage_size log_assemblage_size
            <dbl>               <dbl>
1               5                1.61
2               8                2.08
3              12                2.48
4              18                2.89
5              35                3.56
6              90                4.50
7             250                5.52


The cases have not changed. The numerical scale has.






ImportantTransform the variable, not the evidence



Preserve the original variable so the analytical decision remains transparent and reversible.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
2. Four problems transformations can address
Skewness: log or power transformations can compress a long right tail.
Outlier influence: transformations can pull extreme values inward.
Variance stabilization: transformations can reduce increasing or fan-shaped spread.
Linearizing relationships: transformations can make some curved relationships closer to linear.

skewed <- tibble(x = c(1, 2, 2, 3, 4, 5, 8, 15, 40, 120))
ggplot(skewed, aes(x = x)) + geom_histogram(bins = 8)







ggplot(skewed, aes(x = log(x))) + geom_histogram(bins = 8)














TipDo not transform automatically



A skewed variable is not automatically wrong. Transform when a specific transformation addresses a specific analytical problem and the transformed scale remains meaningful.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
3. Common transformations

Logarithm
For positive values, \(X'=\log(X)\). Logs strongly compress large values, but log(0) is undefined.

x <- c(1, 10, 100, 1000)
log(x)

[1] 0.000000 2.302585 4.605170 6.907755

log(0)

[1] -Inf


Adding a constant in log(X + c) is itself an analytical decision and requires justification.


Square and cube roots

counts <- c(0, 1, 4, 9, 16, 25)
sqrt(counts)

[1] 0 1 2 3 4 5

counts^(1/3)

[1] 0.000000 1.000000 1.587401 2.080084 2.519842 2.924018


Roots are gentler than logs and square roots naturally accommodate zero.


Reciprocal

x <- c(1, 2, 5, 10, 50)
-1 / x

[1] -1.00 -0.50 -0.20 -0.10 -0.02


Reciprocal transformations are much stronger and substantially change interpretation.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
4. Transformation families and standardization
The Box-Cox family considers a spectrum of power transformations for positive data. Familiar points include \(\lambda=1\) (none), \(0.5\) (square root), \(0\) (log), and \(-1\) (inverse). Yeo-Johnson extends similar logic to zero and negative values.
A z-score solves a different problem:
\[z=\frac{X-\bar X}{s}\]

measurements <- c(10, 12, 14, 16, 18)
as.numeric(scale(measurements))

[1] -1.2649111 -0.6324555  0.0000000  0.6324555  1.2649111


Z-scores place variables measured in different units on a common scale; they do not automatically make skewed data normal.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
5. A reproducible transformation workflow
inspect → diagnose → transform → compare → document

Practice 1 — Compare transformations
Create a vector with a long right tail. Compare its raw, square-root, and log histograms. Which transformation compresses the upper tail most strongly? Why should transformation choice depend on more than visual symmetry?


Check your work

The log transformation normally compresses high values more strongly than the square root. Choice depends on analytical purpose, allowable values, and interpretation—not only appearance.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
6. NA is not zero
R represents missing information with NA.

x <- c(4, 7, NA, 12)
x

[1]  4  7 NA 12


NA means unavailable or unknown. It does not tell us what the unobserved value would have been. In archaeology, 0 animal bones can mean a context was examined and none were recorded; NA can mean the context was not examined or the record is unavailable.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
7. Missing values propagate

x <- c(1, 2, NA, 4)
sum(x)

[1] NA

mean(x)

[1] NA

sum(x, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 7

mean(x, na.rm = TRUE)

[1] 2.333333








Warningna.rm = TRUE does not solve missing data



It calculates from observed values. It does not explain why values are missing or establish that observed cases represent missing cases.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
8. Finding missing values
Use is.na(), not == NA.

is.na(x)

[1] FALSE FALSE  TRUE FALSE

sum(is.na(x))

[1] 1

mean(is.na(x))

[1] 0.25



missing_demo <- tibble(
  site = c("A", "B", "C", "D"),
  count = c(12, NA, 0, 8),
  date = c(1200, 1250, NA, 1300)
)
complete.cases(missing_demo)

[1]  TRUE FALSE FALSE  TRUE

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
9. Explicit and implicit missingness
Explicit missingness: the row exists and the cell contains NA.
Implicit missingness: an expected row or combination is absent.

implicit_demo <- tibble(site = "A", period = c(1, 3), value = c(12, 15))
implicit_demo |> complete(site, period = 1:3)

# A tibble: 3 × 3
  site  period value
  <chr>  <dbl> <dbl>
1 A          1    12
2 A          2    NA
3 A          3    15








NoteTwo forms of absence



An explicit missing value is the presence of an absence. An implicit missing value is the absence of an expected presence.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
10. Why is information missing?
MCAR — Missing Completely at Random: missingness is unrelated to observed and unobserved values.
MAR — Missing at Random: missingness depends on other observed variables but, conditional on them, not on the missing value itself.
MNAR — Missing Not at Random: missingness depends on the unobserved value or an unmeasured process connected to it.






ImportantMissingness has a history



In anthropological data, missingness may reflect preservation, excavation, sampling, documentation, literacy, colonial observation, survey participation, or recording practice. Understanding how evidence was produced is part of missing-data analysis.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
11. Deletion and imputation have costs
Listwise deletion removes incomplete cases:

missing_demo |> drop_na()

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  site  count  date
  <chr> <dbl> <dbl>
1 A        12  1200
2 D         8  1300


It reduces sample size and can bias results when missingness is systematic. Pairwise deletion can make different calculations rely on different sample sizes.
Single mean or median imputation makes a dataset look complete but inserts an unobserved constant and tends to reduce variability.
The lecture also introduces multiple imputation conceptually:
incomplete data → several plausible completed datasets → analyze each → pool results






WarningNot required for Assignment 3



Assignment 3 does not require multiple imputation, regression modeling, inferential tests, or other advanced missing-data analysis.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
12. Present, absent, and unknown
Seshat: Global History Databank standardizes historical and archaeological information for large-scale comparison. Whitehouse et al. (2019) used Seshat data to examine social complexity and moralizing gods. For Week 6, the issue is not which broad theory of religion is correct; it is how missing information was represented before analysis.
Beheim et al. (2021) reported the following for the 801 observations used in the statistical tests:



Status
Count
Approximate proportion




documented present
299
37%


documented absent
12
2%


unknown / missing
490
61%



present = evidence of presence
absent = evidence of absence
NA = status unknown

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
13. What happened when NA became 0?
The disputed analysis treated the 490 unknown observations as known absences:
NA  NA  NA  NA  1
 ↓   ↓   ↓   ↓
 0   0   0   0   1
This changes the historical claim. “We do not know” becomes “moralizing gods were absent.” Beheim et al. reported an almost perfect correlation, \(r=0.97\), between missingness and the recoded absence variable.






ImportantAbsence of evidence is not evidence of absence



Turning an unknown historical state into a documented absence is not merely cleaning data. It adds information the original observation did not contain.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
14. Forward bias
Documentation of religious beliefs often depends on written records or literate observers. Earlier or non-literate societies can therefore have more unknown values.
Historical evidence:      NA  NA  NA  →  1
After NA → 0 recoding:     0   0   0  →  1
The second sequence creates a stronger appearance of late emergence than the evidence alone supports. Beheim et al. call this forward bias.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
15. Sensitivity analysis
A sensitivity analysis asks whether the substantive pattern changes when a consequential analytical choice changes.

Analysis A — Unknown remains unknown
Retain NA and summarize documented presence and absence among cases whose status is known.


Analysis B — Unknown becomes absence
Create a new variable in which missing cases are recoded as absence. Do not overwrite the original variable.
If the descriptive conclusion changes substantially, it is sensitive to that decision. If it remains similar, it is more robust to that particular decision.
Sensitivity analysis does not automatically tell you which coding is correct. It tells you whether the conclusion depends on the choice.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
16. Inspect before changing anything
Use the teaching dataset supplied in the Assignment 3 package. Follow the exact filename and variable names in that package’s codebook.

seshat <- read_csv("path/to/assignment03/data/teaching_file.csv")
glimpse(seshat)
summary(seshat)

Identify the unit of observation, relevant variables, coding of documented presence and absence, and all NA values.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
section: 17. Count and visualize the three states

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
18. Preserve both analytical versions
Never overwrite the original variable.

seshat_compare <- seshat |>
  mutate(
    mg_original = moralizing_gods,
    mg_unknown_as_absent = if_else(
      is.na(moralizing_gods), 0, moralizing_gods
    )
  )

Compare Analysis A and Analysis B using summaries, a table, a visualization, or both. Ask how the number and proportion of apparent absences change and whether interpretation changes.

Practice 2 — Why preserve the original?
Why is creating mg_unknown_as_absent safer than replacing moralizing_gods directly?


Check your work

It preserves the source information, makes the recoding visible, allows direct comparison, and prevents an analytical assumption from being mistaken for an original observation.

title: Week 6 — Data Transformation and Missing Values
text:
19. Interpret without overreaching
Assignment 3 asks you to explain why NA and 0 differ, what changes after recoding, whether the descriptive pattern is robust or sensitive, and why absence of evidence differs from evidence of absence.
It does not ask you to reproduce the published statistical models or decide which broader theory of moralizing gods and social complexity is correct.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text: Class meetings: 28 & 30 September 2026 Focus: descriptive statistics · central tendency · dispersion · distribution shape · visualization Practice dataset: Knipper et al. 2020 human stable-isotope data Assessment: Assignment 1 — Bronze Age Diet and Farming at La Bastida and Gatas

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Overview
Week 3 asked how concepts become variables and how research design limits inference. Week 4 asks what to do once a defensible numerical variable has been measured:

How can we describe a distribution without losing the pattern that matters?

Raw observations rarely explain themselves. A list of isotope values, ceramic dimensions, fossil measurements, or survey scores may contain important structure, but that structure is difficult to see until the observations are organized, visualized, and summarized. The Week 4 lecture therefore begins with a simple sequence:
raw observations → summary numbers → empirical pattern → interpretation
Descriptive statistics do not explain why a pattern exists. They make the empirical pattern visible enough that an explanation can later be evaluated.
Two questions organize the entire week:

Central tendency: Where is the distribution centered? What value is typical?
Dispersion / variability: How widely are observations spread around that center?

A center without a measure of spread is incomplete. Two archaeological samples can have the same mean and radically different internal variation. Conversely, two samples can have different means but substantial overlap. This is why the Week 4 lecture treats central tendency and dispersion as a pair rather than as separate topics.
Carlson makes the archaeological version of the same point: the first step in analyzing new data is to look at the data, using numerical summaries, tables, and graphs to identify structure and possible errors before more elaborate analysis begins (Carlson 2017). Banning similarly treats descriptive statistics as a way to summarize both where typical values lie and how “clumped” or dispersed archaeological observations are (Banning 2020).






NoteThe Week 4 principle



Describe before explaining.
A defensible descriptive analysis tells the reader:

what was measured;
what one observation represents;
where the distribution is centered;
how much it varies;
what its shape looks like; and
which observations are unusual.

Only then should we ask why the pattern may exist.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Questions

Why are raw data tables difficult to interpret?
How do descriptive statistics differ from inferential statistics?
Why must the measurement scale be identified before choosing a summary?
When is a mean mathematically computable but substantively meaningless?
How do the mode, median, mean, and trimmed mean define “center” differently?
Why is the mean a balance point or center of gravity?
Why is the median resistant to extreme observations?
What can multimodality reveal?
Why can two samples with the same mean still be very different?
How do range, IQR, variance, standard deviation, MAD, and CV describe different aspects of variability?
Why does sample variance divide by (n-1)?
Why is standard deviation easier to interpret than variance?
When does the 68–95 empirical rule apply?
How do skewness and outliers affect the relationship between mean and median?
What does a boxplot actually show?
Why should an apparent outlier be investigated rather than automatically removed?
When is coefficient of variation useful, and when is it inappropriate?
How are central tendency and dispersion used in archaeology and biological anthropology?
How should human (^{13}) and (^{15}) distributions at La Bastida and Gatas be described?
What can Assignment 1 establish—and what can it not establish?

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: Raw tables do not explain themselves
text:
Raw tables do not explain themselves
A dataset is a collection of observations, not an interpretation.
Carlson emphasizes that archaeological datasets are commonly organized as rectangular tables in which each row represents an observation and each column represents a measurement or attribute of that observation (Carlson 2017). The meaning of a row can change from dataset to dataset: one row might be a survey grid square, a site, a grave, a ceramic sherd, a stone flake, or a human individual.
That means the first questions are not mathematical:

What does one row represent? What does each column represent? How was each variable measured?

Only after those questions are answered do numerical summaries become meaningful.






ImportantA statistic summarizes observations; it does not replace them



Reducing 69 isotope measurements to a mean is useful because it compresses information.
But compression always loses detail.
The goal is therefore not to find one “best number” and discard the distribution. The goal is to combine a small set of summaries with appropriate visualizations so that the center, spread, shape, and unusual observations remain visible.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: A mean can be calculable and meaningless
text:
A mean can be calculable and meaningless
Suppose an artifact-material variable is coded:
Ceramic = 1
Lithic  = 2
Bone    = 3
R can calculate the arithmetic mean of those numbers.
But a “mean artifact material” of 2.13 has no archaeological interpretation because the numbers are merely labels. The distance from ceramic to lithic is not a measured quantitative interval.






NoteNumeric storage is not quantitative meaning



A variable can be stored as numbers in R and still be nominal.
Always distinguish:

how R stores the column, from
what the measurements mean.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: What scale are δ13C and δ15N?
text:
What scale are δ13C and δ15N?
For Assignment 1, human bone-collagen (^{13}) and (^{15}) values are best treated as interval-like measurements for descriptive purposes.
Differences between values are meaningful, but (0‰) is a reference point relative to an isotope standard—not a true absence of carbon or nitrogen isotope composition. Therefore:

means and medians are meaningful;
SD, variance, IQR, and range are meaningful;
ratios such as “twice the δ15N value” are not meaningful; and
CV is not appropriate for the delta values in Assignment 1.







ImportantWhy this matters



Week 4 introduces the coefficient of variation because it is important in anthropology.
But learning a statistic does not mean using it everywhere.
Assignment 1 requires SD, IQR, minimum, maximum, and range—not CV—because the measurement scale and research question do not justify CV for these delta isotope values.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Central tendency summarizes “typical”
A measure of central tendency reduces a distribution to a value intended to represent its center.
The three classical centers are:








Measure
Definition
Particularly useful when




Mode
most frequently occurring value/category
nominal data; discrete peaks; multimodality


Median
50th percentile
ordinal data; skewed data; outliers


Mean
arithmetic average
approximately symmetric interval/ratio data


Trimmed mean
mean after removing equal percentages from both tails
continuous data with influential extremes



Choosing a center is a methodological decision, not a mechanical habit.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: The mode: the most frequent value
text:
The mode: the most frequent value
The mode is the value or category occurring most often.
For categorical variables it may be the only meaningful measure of central tendency.
For continuous archaeological measurements, an exact numerical mode is often less useful because repeated values may depend on measurement precision and rounding. However, modal peaks in a frequency distribution can be archaeologically informative.
The lecture uses standardized stone weights from Mohenjo-Daro as an example: repeated peaks can reveal patterned size classes rather than one smooth continuous distribution.

Unimodal, bimodal, and multimodal
A distribution can have:

one dominant peak — unimodal;
two dominant peaks — bimodal; or
several peaks — multimodal.

Multiple peaks may reflect real subgroups, different production conventions, different populations, or a mixture of processes. They may also arise from small samples or arbitrary histogram bins.






WarningA histogram peak is not automatically a statistical mode



Changing histogram bin width can change the apparent number and location of peaks.
When multimodality matters substantively, inspect the raw values and test whether the apparent structure is robust to reasonable choices of binning.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
The median: the positional center
The median is the middle value after observations are ordered.

50% of observations lie at or below it.
50% lie at or above it.

For an odd number of observations, the median is the middle observation.
For an even number, it is conventionally the average of the two middle observations.
The important property is resistance: the median depends on order, not on how far extreme observations lie from the middle.

x <- c(3, 5, 7, 7, 8)
x_extreme <- c(3, 5, 7, 7, 80)

tibble(
  dataset = c("Original", "One extreme value"),
  mean = c(mean(x), mean(x_extreme)),
  median = c(median(x), median(x_extreme))
)

# A tibble: 2 × 3
  dataset            mean median
  <chr>             <dbl>  <dbl>
1 Original            6        7
2 One extreme value  20.4      7


The extreme value moves the mean much more than the median.
Dressler uses this contrast to show why mean, median, and mode can converge in an approximately symmetric distribution but diverge when a distribution has a long tail (Dressler 2015).

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: The arithmetic mean: the balance point
text:
The arithmetic mean: the balance point
For a sample of (n) observations:
[ {x} = ]
The mean uses every observation.
It can be understood as the distribution’s balance point or center of gravity. If each deviation from the mean is calculated,
[ x_i - {x}, ]
then the deviations sum to zero:
[ _{i=1}^{n}(x_i-{x})=0. ]
This balance property makes the mean fundamental to variance, standard deviation, regression, ANOVA, and many later statistical methods.
Pivitera describes the mean as a balance point rather than necessarily the literal middle observation (Privitera 2024). Dressler similarly presents the mean as a compact model or “best guess” for a value drawn from a roughly symmetric distribution (Dressler 2015).






WarningThe mean is efficient but not resistant



Because every observation contributes to the mean, an extreme observation can pull the balance point toward the tail.
That sensitivity is not a defect to be hidden. It is information about the distribution that should be examined.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: The trimmed mean: a robust compromise
text:
The trimmed mean: a robust compromise
A trimmed mean removes the same proportion of the lowest and highest observations before calculating the mean.
Common trims include 5%, 10%, or 20%.
In R:

x_extreme <- c(3, 5, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12, 80)

mean(x_extreme)

[1] 15.2

mean(x_extreme, trim = 0.10)

[1] 8.625

median(x_extreme)

[1] 8.5


Banning notes that trimmed means can be useful for skewed archaeological distributions or samples containing suspected extremes because they retain much of the data while reducing tail influence (Banning 2020).
A trimmed mean is not required for Assignment 1, but it helps clarify why “center” is not one universal concept.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Why dispersion matters
Suppose two assemblages both have mean artifact length = 50 mm.
One contains measurements tightly concentrated between 48 and 52 mm.
The other ranges from 20 to 80 mm.
The means are identical, but the archaeological patterns are not.
Pivitera emphasizes that variability widens the lens from the center to the structure of the entire distribution (Privitera 2024). Dressler puts the same idea in practical terms: after using a mean as a guess, the next question is how wrong that guess is likely to be (Dressler 2015).

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
The range
The range is:
[ =-. ]
It is easy to understand, but it depends on only two observations.

x <- c(10, 11, 12, 13, 14)
x_outlier <- c(10, 11, 12, 13, 100)

c(
  range_original = max(x) - min(x),
  range_with_outlier = max(x_outlier) - min(x_outlier)
)

    range_original range_with_outlier 
                 4                 90 


The range is therefore fragile:

it is highly sensitive to extreme observations;
it tends to increase as sample size increases; and
it says nothing about how observations are distributed between the minimum and maximum.

Banning makes the archaeological implication explicit: because the range depends only on the two extremes, it is usually a poor stand-alone description of variability (Banning 2020).

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Percentiles and quartiles
A percentile is the value below which a specified percentage of observations lies.
Quartiles divide an ordered distribution into four parts:

(Q_1): 25th percentile;
(Q_2): 50th percentile = median;
(Q_3): 75th percentile.

Each interval between successive quartile boundaries contains roughly one quarter of the observations.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Interquartile range (IQR)
The interquartile range is:
[ IQR = Q_3 - Q_1. ]
It describes the width of the middle 50% of a distribution.
Because it ignores the most extreme quarter at each end, it is much less sensitive to outliers than the total range.
Median + IQR therefore form a natural descriptive pair.

x <- c(3, 5, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 12)

quantile(x, probs = c(0.25, 0.50, 0.75))

25% 50% 75% 
  7   8  10 

IQR(x)

[1] 3


Gonick and Smith’s illustrated treatment makes the same geometry visible: the box in a boxplot runs from (Q_1) to (Q_3), with the median drawn inside (Gonick and Smith 2019).

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: Boxplots: a compact display of center and spread

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: Why simple deviations cannot measure total spread
text:
Why simple deviations cannot measure total spread
The deviation of an observation from the sample mean is:
[ d_i = x_i-{x}. ]
But positive and negative deviations cancel:
[ d_i = 0. ]
So we square them.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Sample variance
For a sample:
[ s^2 = . ]
Variance is the average squared distance around the mean, with the sample correction (n-1).
The numerator,
[ (x_i-{x})^2, ]
is called the sum of squares.
Perkins walks through this logic by subtracting the mean from each value, squaring the deviations, summing them, dividing by (n-1), and then taking the square root to obtain SD (Perkins 2026).

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Why (n-1)?
If the data are treated as a sample used to estimate population variability, dividing by (n) tends to underestimate the population variance.
Using (n-1) is the familiar Bessel correction.
R’s:
var(x)
sd(x)
use the sample formulas with (n-1).
For Assignment 1, that is exactly what students should use.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Standard deviation
The standard deviation is:
[ s=. ]
Variance has squared units:

mm²;
g²;
‰².

Taking the square root returns the result to the original measurement units.
That is why SD is generally easier to interpret than variance.
Dressler emphasizes this return to the original metric: the squaring needed to construct variance makes the units difficult to interpret, while the square root restores them (Dressler 2015).






NoteInterpret SD as spread, not as a guaranteed boundary



A larger SD means observations are, on average, more dispersed around the mean.
It does not mean every observation falls within one SD of the mean.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Median absolute deviation (MAD)
A robust alternative to SD is the median absolute deviation:
[ MAD = (|x_i-(x)|). ]
Like the median and IQR, MAD is resistant to extreme observations.
In R, note an important detail:

x <- c(3, 5, 7, 7, 8, 9, 10, 11, 80)

# Raw median absolute deviation from the median:
mad(x, constant = 1)

[1] 2

# R's default is scaled to estimate SD under normality:
mad(x)

[1] 2.9652


MAD is not required for Assignment 1, but it provides a useful comparison when distributions are strongly skewed or contain influential extremes.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Coefficient of variation (CV)
For an appropriate ratio-scale variable:
[ CV=%. ]
CV expresses variability relative to the magnitude of the mean.
This matters when absolute SD naturally increases with body size or scale.

Bioanthropological application
Plavcan shows why relative variability matters in studies of living primates and fossil hominins. An SD measured in grams or millimeters will naturally be larger for a large-bodied species than for a small-bodied species, even if their relative variability is similar (Plavcan 2012).
The CV places variation on a relative scale.
Plavcan’s comparative data also show why simple universal cutoffs are dangerous: within-sex variation differs by trait. Many craniofacial dimensions in living primates have CVs below 10%, while body-mass CVs can be around 12–15%; fossil interpretation must also consider geography, time, sex, taxonomy, sample quality, and trait choice (Plavcan 2012).






WarningCV is not a universal standardization detector



The lecture uses CV to illustrate technological standardization and biological size variation.
A low CV can be consistent with standardized production, but it does not by itself prove specialist production.
Sampling, raw material, function, measurement protocol, temporal mixing, and the scale of the mean can all affect observed variability.




Why Assignment 1 does not use CV
Assignment 1 compares (^{13}) and (^{15}) delta values.
Because their zero points are reference points rather than true absence, a ratio such as (s/{x}) does not have the interpretation required for CV.
Use the assignment’s requested measures:

SD;
IQR;
minimum;
maximum; and
range.

A right-skewed distribution has a long tail toward larger values.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: Skewness is a clue, not a verdict
text:
Skewness is a clue, not a verdict
Mean–median differences can signal asymmetry, but they are not a complete diagnostic.
Always inspect the distribution itself.
Perkins’s R chapter demonstrates why: a histogram reveals tail structure and unusual observations that a table of descriptive statistics can summarize but cannot fully display (Perkins 2026).






NotePair the statistic with the picture



A useful Week 4 habit is:
histogram → boxplot → numerical summaries → interpretation
not:
mean → conclusion.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Archaeological standardization
Archaeologists can compare dispersion in:

ceramic dimensions;
projectile-point measurements;
brick sizes;
weight systems; or
other manufactured objects.

A tightly clustered distribution may be consistent with stronger standardization; a broader distribution may indicate greater heterogeneity.
But Banning’s larger methodological warning remains essential: apparent variation can also arise from measurement protocol, analyst decisions, sampling, classification, or the archaeological formation process (Banning 2020).
Thus:

variation becomes archaeological evidence only after we understand how the variation was produced.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: Means can also be misleading because of measurement decisions
text:
Means can also be misleading because of measurement decisions
Banning gives an especially important archaeological example: average artifact size depends on what counts as a measurable artifact. If one analyst includes fragments down to 1 cm and another includes only pieces above 2 cm, they can obtain different means from the same underlying material (Banning 2020).
The lesson connects Week 3 to Week 4:

descriptive statistics inherit every decision built into measurement and sampling.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: El Argar, La Bastida, and Gatas
text:
El Argar, La Bastida, and Gatas
Assignment 1 is based on Knipper et al.’s study of the El Argar society of southeast Iberia, approximately 2200–1550 cal BCE (Knipper et al. 2020).
El Argar was a complex Bronze Age society characterized by:

fortified settlements;
cereal agriculture;
metallurgy;
hierarchical social organization; and
marked funerary inequality.

The study compares La Bastida and Gatas, two hilltop settlements with social, economic, and environmental differences.
Knipper and colleagues analyzed several positions in the food web:

cereals → domestic animals → humans

They measured stable carbon and nitrogen isotope composition in charred cereal grains and in animal and human bone collagen (Knipper et al. 2020).
This broader design matters because the Assignment 1 teaching file contains only the human observations.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
The usable human sample
The original study sampled 75 humans:

52 from La Bastida;
23 from Gatas.

Six samples were excluded from interpretation because collagen preservation was insufficient.
The evaluable human results are therefore:

La Bastida: 48
Gatas: 21
Total: 69

These 69 observations form the Assignment 1 teaching dataset (Knipper et al. 2020).

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
section: What δ13C and δ15N can tell us

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
The crucial archaeological lesson
The human values at La Bastida are higher on average for both (^{13}) and (^{15}) than at Gatas in the original study (Knipper et al. 2020).
A tempting interpretation would be:

Higher human (^{15}) at La Bastida = more meat or dairy.

The full food-web evidence makes that inference unsafe.
Knipper et al. found differences in cereal and animal baselines as well. Their results indicate extensive rain-fed cereal cultivation with little to moderate manuring, and especially at La Bastida they found strong integration between crop production and domestic-animal feeding. When plant and animal baselines are considered, higher human isotope values do not necessarily imply different average dietary composition (Knipper et al. 2020).






ImportantAssignment 1 is intentionally narrower than the published paper



Your task is not to reproduce Knipper et al.’s complete dietary reconstruction.
Your task is to establish:

What do the observed human isotope distributions show?

Only after describing the distributions should you discuss archaeological interpretations that are consistent with the evidence.

n
How many non-missing observations contributed to that site × isotope summary?

The arithmetic balance point.
Ask whether extreme values appear to pull it away from the main body of the distribution.


median
The 50th percentile.
Ask whether it differs meaningfully from the mean.


sd
The sample standard deviation.
It is expressed in the same unit as the isotope measurement: ‰.


iqr
The width of the middle 50%.
It is resistant to the tails and pairs naturally with the median.


min, max, and range
These describe the extremes and total observed span.

Step 11 — Compare SD with IQR
SD and IQR do not measure exactly the same thing, so do not compare their raw magnitudes as if they should be equal.
Instead ask:

Does the boxplot show a compact middle 50% but long tails?
Does the range look large relative to the IQR?
Are one or two observations influencing the SD?
Are the data reasonably symmetric so that mean + SD give a useful compact description?
Would median + IQR more faithfully represent the center and central spread?







NoteThere is no rule that you must choose only one pair



A good descriptive report can present both:

mean + SD; and
median + IQR

when they reveal different aspects of the distribution.
Assignment 1 asks you to calculate both so that you can explain what each contributes.

Step 13 — Describe first, interpret second
A strong Assignment 1 paragraph has two stages.

Stage A — Statistical description
Describe only what the human distributions show.
A useful template is:

For (^{15}), the La Bastida sample had a [higher/lower/similar] center than Gatas. The mean and median were [close/different], while the SD and IQR indicate [greater/lower/similar] variability. The histogram and boxplot show [symmetry/skew/tails/overlap/unusual observations].

Use your actual output to replace the bracketed phrases.


Stage B — Archaeological interpretation
Then explain what is consistent with the pattern while respecting the limits of the assignment.
A useful transition is:

These descriptive differences demonstrate variation in the human isotope distributions, but they do not by themselves identify the dietary or agricultural mechanism that produced it.

Then bring in Knipper et al.’s wider plant–animal–human evidence (Knipper et al. 2020).

section: Step 14 — Answer the assignment’s four interpretive questions
text:
Step 14 — Answer the assignment’s four interpretive questions

1. What is the unit of analysis?
One sampled human individual.


2. What descriptive statistical result matters most?
There is no single answer supplied in advance.
Choose the result that most clearly characterizes the important empirical pattern and justify the choice using the visualizations and summary statistics.


3. What archaeological or anthropological interpretation is consistent with the distributions?
Your interpretation should be cautious and contextual.
The human distributions can be discussed in relation to the broader El Argar food-web study, but the Assignment 1 data alone do not reconstruct the entire food system.


4. What claim do these descriptive data alone not support?
Examples of claims that would require additional evidence include:

exact proportions of meat, dairy, barley, or other foods;
a causal claim that site status produced isotope differences;
a claim that higher (^{15}) necessarily means more animal protein;
a population-wide claim about all inhabitants of La Bastida or Gatas;
a causal claim about manuring or irrigation from the human dataset alone.

text:
Exercise 1 — Which center?

Consider:
3, 5, 7, 7, 8, 9, 80
Without using R:

Which value will affect the mean most?
Will the median change dramatically because of the value 80?
Which center better describes a “typical” observation here?
What additional plot would you want to see before making a final decision?








TipCheck your reasoning





The value 80 strongly affects the mean but has much less influence on the median.
The median is therefore more resistant for this strongly right-tailed toy dataset.
A histogram, dot plot, or boxplot would help show whether 80 is isolated from the main body of observations.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Exercise 2 — Same mean, different spread

Compare:
a <- c(8, 9, 10, 11, 12)
b <- c(0, 5, 10, 15, 20)

Calculate the mean of each.
Calculate the SD of each.
What would be lost if you reported only the means?








TipCheck with R





mean(a)
mean(b)

sd(a)
sd(b)
The means are the same, but the second dataset is much more dispersed.
This is why central tendency without dispersion is incomplete.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Exercise 3 — Range versus IQR

Start with:
x <- c(10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16)
Then replace 16 with 100.
Compare:

range;
IQR.

Which statistic changes more, and why?







TipCheck with R





x1 <- c(10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 16)
x2 <- c(10, 11, 12, 13, 14, 15, 100)

max(x1) - min(x1)
max(x2) - min(x2)

IQR(x1)
IQR(x2)
The range depends directly on the extreme values, whereas the IQR focuses on the middle 50%.

text:
Exercise 5 — Choose the summary pair

For each hypothetical distribution, choose the most informative primary pair:

mean + SD, or
median + IQR.


A
Symmetric, unimodal, no influential extremes.


B
Strong right skew with several high values.


C
Ordinal preservation scores: poor / fair / good / excellent.
Explain your choices.








TipCheck your reasoning






A: mean + SD is usually efficient and interpretable.
B: median + IQR is more resistant, though reporting both pairs can reveal the effect of the tail.
C: median + IQR is compatible with ordered categories; an arithmetic mean assumes quantitative intervals not supplied by the labels.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Exercise 6 — Is CV appropriate?

Would CV be appropriate for:

femoral-head diameter in mm?
body mass in kg?
(^{15}) reported in ‰ relative to a standard?
temperature in °C?

Explain the measurement-scale reason for each answer.







TipCheck your reasoning





CV requires a ratio scale with a meaningful nonzero mean.
It is defensible for femoral-head diameter and body mass.
It is not appropriate for delta isotope values or Celsius temperature because their zero points are reference points rather than true absence.

title: Week 4 — Measures of Central Tendency and Dispersion
text:
Exercise 7 — Separate description from explanation

Rewrite this sentence so that statistical description and archaeological explanation are separated:

“La Bastida people ate more meat because their mean δ15N is higher.”

Your revision should contain:

one descriptive sentence; and
one cautious interpretive sentence.








TipOne defensible structure





A stronger structure is:

The La Bastida human sample has higher δ15N values on average than the Gatas sample.

Then:

This descriptive difference does not by itself demonstrate greater meat consumption, because isotope baselines also vary across crops and animals; the wider food-web evidence is needed to evaluate the mechanism.

The exact wording should reflect your own Assignment 1 results and reading of Knipper et al. (Knipper et al. 2020).

title: Week 2 — Using R, RStudio, and Quarto
text:
Overview
This week is about learning a workflow, not memorizing commands.
R is the language we will use to work with data. RStudio is the environment in which we will organize and run that work. Quarto is the document system that brings prose, R code, results, tables, figures, and citations together in a reproducible report (Tierney 2025).
By the end of the week, you should be able to open an RStudio project, understand the basic structure of an R command, create and inspect R objects, import a CSV file, use a small set of tidyverse verbs, create a first ggplot2 figure, and render a Quarto document from a clean R session.






NoteThe Week 2 principle



Do not separate “doing the analysis” from “documenting the analysis.”
In ANTH418, the code that produces a result should live beside the explanation of what the result means.

What are R, RStudio, and Quarto, and how do they differ?

What do select(), filter(), mutate(), summarise(), group_by(), and |> do?
How does a Quarto document turn code and prose into a reproducible HTML page?

title: Week 2 — Using R, RStudio, and Quarto
text:
Before class: install the software
ANTH418 assumes no previous programming experience. Before beginning the exercises below, make sure that R and RStudio are installed and working on your computer.
The three names can be confusing at first:

R is the language that performs the computation. RStudio is the application in which we will write and organize most of our R work. Quarto turns our code, results, figures, and writing into a reproducible document.


Step 1 — Install R
Download R from the Comprehensive R Archive Network (CRAN):
https://cran.r-project.org/
Choose the installer for your operating system:

macOS: choose Download R for macOS and install the current release appropriate for your Mac;
Windows: choose Download R for Windows → base → the current release; or
Linux: follow the instructions for your distribution.

Use the standard/default installation options unless you have a specific reason to change them.






NoteR must be installed before RStudio



RStudio does not replace R. It provides an easier environment for working with R, but it still needs an R installation on your computer.




Step 2 — Install RStudio Desktop
Download the free RStudio Desktop from Posit:
https://posit.co/download/rstudio-desktop/
Install the current stable release for your operating system.
On first launch, RStudio should normally find your R installation automatically.
Current versions of RStudio include integrated support for Quarto and bundle a stable Quarto release. For most ANTH418 students, installing current R and current RStudio is therefore enough to begin working with .qmd files.


Step 3 — Check Quarto
After installing RStudio, open it and choose the Terminal tab. Run:
quarto --version
You should see a version number.
Then run:
quarto check
This checks whether Quarto can find the software it needs, including R and the Knitr execution engine.






TipDo I need to install Quarto separately?



Usually no if you have installed a current release of RStudio, because RStudio bundles Quarto.
If quarto --version does not work, or if you need a newer standalone Quarto release, install it from:
https://quarto.org/docs/get-started/
After installation, restart RStudio and run quarto --version again.




Step 4 — Install the R packages used in ANTH418
Packages extend what R can do. For the first part of the course, the main package collection we need is the tidyverse.
In the R Console, run:
install.packages("tidyverse")
You normally install a package only once on a computer.
Then test that it loads:
library(tidyverse)
If the command finishes without an error, the package is available.






ImportantConsole or Terminal?



RStudio contains both, but they serve different purposes.

Use the R Console for R commands such as install.packages() and library().
Use the Terminal for system commands such as quarto --version and quarto check.

We will use both during the course.




Step 5 — Verify the complete setup
In the R Console, run:
R.version.string
1 + 1
library(tidyverse)
You should see your R version, the result 2, and no error when the tidyverse loads.
In the Terminal, run:
quarto --version
If those checks work, you have the basic ANTH418 computational environment.


Step 6 — Make a tiny Quarto test document
In RStudio choose:
File → New File → Quarto Document…
Choose HTML and create the document. Replace its body with:
## My first R calculation


::: {.cell}

```{.r .cell-code}
2 + 2
```

::: {.cell-output .cell-output-stdout}

```
[1] 4
```


:::
:::
Save the file as something like:
quarto_test.qmd
Then click Render.
If an HTML page appears showing both the code and the result 4, then R, RStudio, Knitr, and Quarto are communicating correctly.






NoteYou do not need every optional tool



quarto check may report that tools such as TinyTeX, Jupyter, or Julia are not installed. That is fine for the R-based HTML work in ANTH418.
Do not install extra software simply to make every optional check appear as installed.




If installation fails
Do not spend hours troubleshooting alone. Record:

your operating system;
the exact error message;
what you were trying to install or run; and
a screenshot if useful.

Bring that information to class or office hours. Error messages are evidence: copy them exactly rather than paraphrasing them.

title: Week 2 — Using R, RStudio, and Quarto
text:
R, RStudio, and Quarto

R
R is a programming language and statistical computing environment.
When you write
mean(c(4, 7, 9))
R evaluates the instruction and returns a result.
R is where the computation happens.


RStudio
RStudio is an integrated development environment (IDE). It gives you a convenient place to work with R:

the Source pane for scripts and Quarto documents;
the Console for commands and output;
the Environment pane for objects currently in memory;
the Files / Plots / Packages / Help panes for navigating the project and inspecting results; and
project tools that help keep files, code, and working directories organized.

An RStudio Project is especially important because it gives a project a stable root directory. Project-based organization prevents many file-path problems and makes analyses more portable (Tierney 2025).


Quarto
Quarto is a scientific and technical publishing system.
A Quarto document can contain:

Markdown prose;
executable R code;
tables;
figures;
equations;
citations; and
cross-references.

The .qmd source is the document you edit. Rendering turns it into an output such as HTML, PDF, or Word.






TipA useful mental model



R computes. RStudio organizes. Quarto communicates reproducibly.

title: Week 2 — Using R, RStudio, and Quarto
text:
Projects and file paths
A reproducible analysis should not depend on a path that only exists on your own computer.
Avoid code such as:
# Do not write paths like this in course work:
read_csv("/Users/yourname/Desktop/my-course/data/file.csv")
and avoid beginning an analysis with:
setwd("/Users/yourname/some/very/specific/location")
Instead, open the relevant RStudio Project and work with relative paths:
read_csv("data/file.csv")
This is one of the workflow practices emphasized in Quarto for Scientists: keep the files for one project together and let the project establish a stable starting point for your analysis (Tierney 2025).

Inspect your current project
Run these commands in the Console:

getwd()
list.files()
file.exists("data")


Your turn — read a file path.
In the path data/knipper2020_humans.csv:

What is the directory?
What is the file?
Is the path absolute or relative?
Why is this path more portable than one beginning with /Users/...?

Your first R commands
R can be used like a calculator:

[1] 9


Lines beginning with # are comments:
# R ignores this line.
# Comments should explain why the code is doing something useful.

Assignment: creating objects
Use <- to assign a value to an object:

site_name <- "La Bastida"
n_individuals <- 48
has_isotope_data <- TRUE

site_name

[1] "La Bastida"

n_individuals

[1] 48

has_isotope_data

The object name is on the left. The value is on the right.






ImportantObjects exist in the current R session



Creating n_individuals <- 48 does not permanently save that value inside R.
For a reproducible analysis, the code that creates an object should be written in your script or .qmd document so it can be recreated when the document is rendered.
